Also, since many modern laptops only have USB-C video outputs, they can't connect to most KVM switches without a dock or adapter, because most KVM switches only come with HDMI and DisplayPort inputs. A USB dock can plug into that USB-C port and let you connect the laptop to any monitor or KVM switch, while also packing a bunch of extra ports you can use as you please. | | USB dock | KVM switch | |---|---|---| | What it does | Adds ports | Shares peripherals | | Connects to | One computer | Two or more computers | | What you connect to it | Monitors, Ethernet, SD cards, USB devices, and more | Keyboard, mouse, monitor, sometimes audio and USB devices | | Best for | Laptops and handheld PCs | People with multiple PCs | In other words, you don't have to limit yourself to one or the other. If you need both, you can use them together and get the best of both worlds. The dock lets you connect your laptop to a KVM switch with a regular HDMI cable, or to a monitor with a built-in KVM switch with a USB-C cable, while still giving you a bunch of extra ports for peripherals, SD cards, speakers, Ethernet, and more. I use both, and I'm never going back While I'd managed to use my Windows desktop and Mac mini with a single monitor and a single set of peripherals without a KVM switch (my mouse and keyboard both support Bluetooth), getting a monitor with one built-in really simplified my setup. Both my mouse's wireless dongle and my keyboard's cable are now plugged into the monitor, and they magically switch between the two PCs with a few button presses. The only thing I still have to do is toggle my speakers between wired and Bluetooth mode whenever I change computers. On top of that, I use a Thunderbolt docking station with the Mac mini, and I love it. It's made the mini even more versatile than my desktop PC, since the dock comes with an SD card slot and multiple Thunderbolt ports I can use to charge my phone, mouse, wireless earbuds, and other gadgets. If you ask me, combining a USB dock and a KVM switch is the way to go, and I'm never going back to my old desk setup.

item.title: This Ethernet cable test tells you more than a speed test ever will
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.40
If you feel like your internet is playing up, what's the first thing you do? A lot of us reach for the same tool: a speed test. Those things catch more than just slow internet; they also note your latency, and if there's packet loss, you'll see it because the speed test will take ages to complete (or it won't complete at all). And as long as it shows a number within our expectations, we shrug and assume the Wi-Fi is just having a bad day. A simple speed test, however, is not something anyone should be judging their whole network by. Even with a half-dead Ethernet cable, for example, your speed test can still give you a good result. If you actually want to test your setup, a bandwidth test is the better place to start. A speed test only ever checks your internet, not your cable It taps out the second you hit whatever your plan is selling you All a speed test does is measure the path from your device to a server on the internet, and it's completely capped by whatever internet plan you have. Ethernet cables, however, can move much faster than most plans, so a speed test will likely never stress it. If you do end up with a low number from a speed test, guessing the culprit can be pretty difficult. It could be your ISP, a VPN, a browser extension, a busy test server, congestion, an old router, or something else entirely. It's also worth going around and checking your Ethernet cables, since you could be dealing with something like a broken locking clip, a sharp bend, or a chewed cable. If you have pets, that can definitely happen; I still remember years ago, when my (then a puppy) dog chewed up my Ethernet cable in a fairly hidden-away spot. It took me a while to notice. There are honestly so many things that can cause a bad speed test result. It's not always your ISP (although in my case, it often is, but I'm unlucky when it comes to ISPs). The sneaky part is how a bad cable actually fails Gigabit needs all four pairs, and losing one won't kill the connection An Ethernet cable has eight wires inside, arranged as four twisted pairs. Full gigabit (the 1000BASE-T standard) needs all four of those pairs in working order, while older 100Mbps Fast Ethernet only needs two. So, if one pair gets damaged, your link can drop from 1Gbps down to 100Mbps but keep working all the same. Nothing disconnects, nothing throws an error, and the connection simply renegotiates itself down to stay stable. If things go really wrong, your adapter can even negotiate itself down to 2003-era speeds without you noticing a thing. The actual test: check your link speed, then run iPerf3 One number shows you the ceiling, the other shows you what you're getting The first thing to check is your link speed, also called the negotiated speed. On Windows, head to Settings, then Network & internet, then Ethernet, or just run Get-NetAdapter in PowerShell. If your PC has a gigabit port but the link only shows 100Mbps, then the problem is somewhere in your wiring rather than your internet. (Potentially. Maybe. Network troubleshooting is such a hassle, honestly.) Next, try out this great tool: iPerf3. I use it a lot. It's a free command-line utility that measures raw speed between two devices on your own network, with the internet completely out of the picture. Instead, it shows you the true ceiling of your cable, port, and network card. Install it on two devices (brew install iperf3 on Mac, Scoop or winget on Windows, apt on Linux). On one machine, run iperf3 -s to make it the server, then on the other, run iperf3 -c followed by the first machine's IP address. A healthy cable should give you around 900Mbps or more, so if you're crawling at under 100Mbps instead, you have discovered a faulty cable. Tack on -R to flip the direction, -t 30 for a longer run, or -i 1 to catch intermittent drops, and keep an eye on the "Retr" column, since a pile of retransmits usually means a flaky physical link. When the test finally points at the cable Swap first, tester second, replace third So, if these tests come up with bad results, the fix is pretty straightforward. First, verify the results by swapping in a short, working cable, and run the test again. If the numbers jump up, that cable is definitely the problem. It's the same trick I use for a cable that might simply be too long, where the signal degrades just enough to force those same slowdowns. A cheap cable tester (the $10 kind) is a good next step, since it instantly catches broken wires, shorts, and miswires. Just know it won't flag subtler issues like crosstalk, so a cable can technically "pass" and still choke at gigabit. As for replacements, Cat6 should be the default for anything new, but there's definitely no need to panic-buy Cat8 for a normal home. Honestly, plenty of the Cat5e cables you already own are still perfectly fine for gigabit, as long as they're in good shape. The speed test isn't useless, it's just answering a different question A speed test tells you if you're getting the internet speeds you're paying for, and that's something we all need to check at one point or another. Your link speed and an iPerf3 run, however, answer a completely different question: "Is my own wiring quietly holding me back?" Nothing lasts forever, so at some point, those Ethernet cables will be the ones causing the problems.

item.title: 7 Windows features I disabled after realizing nobody needs to use them
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.18
Despite legions of fellow nerds exclaiming the virtues of Linux or macOS, I still actively choose Microsoft’s Windows. I do so for the same reason I elect to play video games on my console instead of my more expensive, capable, powerful, and modular desktop: convenience. Windows 11 is far from perfect, though, and many default features and apps can be disabled to reduce clutter, improve performance, and make your computer better for you. So, here are seven lucky ways to optimize Windows 11, even if you don't consider yourself a computer-using expert. OneDrive cloud syncing Keep your files local OneDrive lives on your taskbar, in your apps list, and all over File Explorer. The idea is perfect integration that syncs all your files to the cloud, but not everyone uses OneDrive for their cloud storage needs, and plenty of people don't want a cloud storage solution at all. OneDrive may seem like a permanent fixture in Windows 11, but it's actually easy to remove. For one, you can simply unlink your Microsoft account and disable OneDrive without removing it. - Open the File Explorer app (you can use the Win + E keyboard shortcut). - Navigate to the OneDrive folder in the left-hand navigation menu (should be named something like "Your name" - Personal). - Click on OneDrive in the address bar at the top. - Click on the Settings icon in the lower right-hand corner. - Navigate to Account in the left-hand navigation menu. - Click Unlink this PC. - Confirm your choice to complete the process. Alternatively, you can remove OneDrive from your PC completely (you can always reinstall it later if you'd like). Any local files you had synced to or from OneDrive will remain on your PC. - Open the Settings app (you can use the Win + I keyboard shortcut). - Navigate to Apps in the left-hand navigation menu. - Navigate to Installed apps on this page. - Find Microsoft OneDrive in this list. - Click the right-hand three-dot ellipsis icon. - Click Uninstall. - Follow the prompts to complete the uninstall process. Copilot companion Avoid the AI craze Microsoft really wants you to use its Copilot AI companion, which is built into Windows 11, integrated into multiple Microsoft apps, a part of Office and PC branding, and even takes up an entire key on new keyboards. Fortunately, newer versions of Windows 11 also make it much easier to remove the base Copilot from your computer. - Open the Settings app. - Navigate to Apps in the left-hand navigation menu. - Navigate to Installed apps on this page. - Find Copilot in this list. - Click the right-hand three-dot ellipsis icon. - Click Uninstall. - Follow the prompts to complete the uninstall process. Yes, you can absolutely repeat the above process with the Microsoft 365 Copilot app to reduce AI integration in your Office apps (and you can still use all your standard Office apps like normal). You can also now change the function of the Copilot key on your keyboard — and the Win + C keyboard shortcut — without installing any new apps or going into the Registry Editor. - Open the Settings app. - Navigate to Bluetooth & devices in the left-hand navigation menu. - Navigate to Keyboard on this page. - Find Customize Copilot key on keyboard under Shortcuts and hotkeys. - Click the right-hand drop-down menu and choose Search (to open Windows Search) or Open an app (to choose the app you want). Widgets and news Who even uses this? Another addition to Windows 11 that most people never touch is the Widgets board, which takes up the left-hand side of your taskbar with weather, financial updates, and breaking news. Accidentally hover over it, and it'll open a poorly curated news feed and various app widgets that you can add, remove, and move around. If you value having the actual widgets, there are still ways to improve the Widgets board without removing it. - Open the Widgets board by hovering over or clicking the left-hand area of the taskbar. - Click the Settings icon in the upper right-hand corner. - If you'd like to make the Widgets board only open when you click it, toggle the Open Widgets board on hover to Off. - If you'd like to remove the news feed entirely and only have actual widgets, navigate to Show or hide feeds on this page. - Toggle Feed to Off (if you have installed alternative news feeds, they'll also show up here). - Confirm your choice to complete the process. For those who'd rather remove the Widgets board altogether, that's also possible. - Open the Settings app. - Navigate to Personalization in the left-hand navigation menu. - Navigate to Taskbar on this page. - Find Widgets under Taskbar items and toggle it Off. Start Menu bloat There's a lot you can improve here The latest Start Menu design in Windows 11 is a major improvement over previous iterations in terms of customizability and intuitiveness, but there are still plenty of features and elements that are enabled by default. If you want a clean, straightforward Start Menu that gets you to your apps as quickly as possible, here are some tips. - Open the Settings app. - Navigate to Personalization in the left-hand navigation menu. - Navigate to Start on this page. - To remove the pinned section for apps, toggle Pinned to Off. - To remove the dynamic section for recent apps, file suggestions, and tips from the Start Menu, toggle Recent to Off (or customize the individual options). - To remove the Phone Link panel from the Start Menu, toggle Show mobile device in Start to Off. - To disable notifications in the Start Menu, toggle Show account-related notifications to Off. Phone Link integration This feature shows up everywhere You can connect your phone to your PC to access messages, make phone calls, use apps, and even share files and photos in Windows 11, but Phone Link isn't a useful feature for everyone. More importantly, it stays active and uses background resources even if you don't set it up, and it's deeply integrated into Windows 11, so it's not easy to remove. Fortunately, there are three things you can do (aside from hiding it from the Start Menu, as I mentioned in the last section) to keep Phone Link (and all related cross-device sharing features) out of your RAM and your way. - Open the Settings app. - Navigate to Bluetooth & devices in the left-hand navigation menu. - Navigate to Mobile devices on this page. - Toggle Allow this PC to access content and capabilities from your mobile devices to Off. - Toggle Show me suggestions for using my mobile device with Windows to Off. - Navigate to Apps in the left-hand navigation menu. - Navigate to Startup on this page. - Toggle Mobile devices to Off. - Toggle Phone Link to Off. - Return to Apps. - Navigate to Resume on this page. - Toggle Resume to Off. If you'd like to completely uninstall the Phone Link application, you can do so using Windows PowerShell in the Terminal, as there's no easy way through Windows 11's Settings. - Find the Terminal app using the Start Menu or Windows Search. - Right-click the Terminal app and click Run as administrator. - Click Yes on the prompt to open the Terminal app. - Copy and paste the following command: Get-AppxPackage Microsoft.YourPhone -AllUsers | Remove-AppxPackage. - Press the Enter key and wait for the process to complete (Phone Link should be completely uninstalled, but you may need to restart your PC to remove it from the Start Menu list of installed apps). Xbox gaming features Not everyone is a gamer Xbox is a major part of the Microsoft ecosystem, and it's understandably deeply integrated into Windows 11. If you don't plan to use those Xbox gaming features (or game at all), you can free up resources and clean up your computer by removing or disabling them. - Open the Settings app. - Navigate to Apps in the left-hand navigation menu. - Navigate to Installed apps on this page. - Find Xbox in this list. - Click the right-hand three-dot ellipsis icon. - Click Uninstall. - Find Xbox Live in this list. - Click the right-hand three-dot ellipsis icon. - Click Uninstall. - Navigate to Gaming in the left-hand navigation menu. - Navigate to Game Mode on this page. - Toggle Game Mode to Off. The Gaming section of Settings has other options, but they don't matter if you uninstall all the Xbox apps. That includes the Xbox Game Bar, which is unfortunately more difficult to remove from Windows 11, as it's treated as a system component (like Phone Link). That doesn't mean it's impossible, though! - Find the Terminal app using the Start Menu or Windows Search - Right-click the Terminal app and click Run as administrator - Click Yes on the prompt to open the Terminal app - Check that you're in a Windows PowerShell tab or open a new tab by pressing Ctrl + Shift + 1 - Copy and paste the following command: Get-AppxPackage Microsoft.XboxGamingOverlay -AllUsers | Remove-AppxPackage - Press the Enter key and wait for the process to complete (Game Bar should be completely uninstalled, but you may need to restart your PC to remove it from the Start Menu list of installed apps) Search web results Drop Bing to speed up searches My final suggestion is to massively improve the performance and consistency of scouring your apps and files with Windows Search in the Start Menu, on the taskbar, or by pressing Win + S. Many Windows users (myself included) have experienced slow load times and annoyingly irrelevant web results when looking for something, but it's possible to completely remove Bing and internet-connected web results from your computer's Windows Search feature. You can dive into the Registry Editor if you're confident, but I'll make it much easier and give you a way to do so with Windows PowerShell. - Find the Terminal app using the Start Menu or Windows Search. - Right-click the Terminal app and click Run as administrator. - Click Yes on the prompt to open the Terminal app. - Check that you're in a Windows PowerShell tab or open a new tab by pressing Ctrl + Shift + 1. - Copy and paste the following command: New-Item -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer" -Force | Out-Null; New-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer" -Name "DisableSearchBoxSuggestions" -Value 1 -PropertyType DWord -Force | Out-Null. - Press the Enter key and wait for the process to complete. - Restart your computer. Windows 11 is great, but it feels awfully bloated sometimes Decades of iteration and updates have made Windows 11 incredibly powerful and packed with an endless array of features (especially if you're invested in Microsoft's ecosystem), but many of the features you're not using may be slowing down your computer, taking up precious storage or memory, and getting in your way. Disabling or removing the seven features listed above results in a much cleaner Windows 11 experience.

item.title: I tested 3 paper-like Android tablets, and the winner isn't e-ink
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.38
As much as I enjoy digital books and comics, there is nothing quite like reading on paper—but I have neither the budget nor the space to amass physical copies of my digital library. This is why I've kept tabs on the state of paper-like Android tablets over the years. After comparing three devices that each take a different approach, here's what I would buy. A black and white E Ink tablet My BOOX Go 10.3 is great for books and manga, but color comics are a no-go When I read a digital copy of a novel on my super-thin BOOX Go 10.3, it's increasingly hard to argue that it isn't a superior experience to carrying around a physical book. The text looks as crisp as on paper, except I have complete freedom to change the size, font, and spacing. It's gentle on my eyes and ideal for reading outdoors. The device itself is paper-thin, which can't be said for the physical versions of the lengthy fantasy ebooks I'm currently reading (Adrian Tchaikovsky’s Epic Fantasy bundle has been a banger). Reading manga or other black and white comics on this device feels just as good. The lines are striking, providing amazing contrast without the eye strain that comes from staring at a mostly white OLED or LCD. If you have the opportunity to read Strangers in Paradise on a monochrome E Ink tablet, do it. Tragically, things tend to fall apart when I want to read my full-color comics. A monochromatic eReader like my BOOX Go can only render these in black and white, which loses much of the detail and often isn't fully legible. This leads me to try a color eReader instead. A color E Ink tablet I found the Bigme B10 an okay comic experience and worse for everything else My first color E Ink eReader was the BOOX Tab Ultra C. On that device, color E ink felt like reading newspaper prints. It's not a bad look, but it's also not the one that series like Saga or Monstress were designed for. These comics look much more accurately represented on the OLED screen of my Motorola Razr Fold than they do on an E Iink tablet. This year, I tried out a Bigme B10. Despite being a newer tablet with better specs, the technology hasn't evolved in the past few years. In fact, this purchase was a step backward. Bigme's software is so janky that I very quickly sold the device (Bigme’s return policy was too costly and time-consuming to bother). If anything, the color representation on the comics I wanted to read felt worse than I remembered and not worth the roughly $600 this device commanded. It gets worse. Color Kaleido 3 screens are incredibly dim, so they require a front light in all but direct light. Their lower contrast also makes ebooks less pleasant to read than they are on black and white eReaders. The end-result is a display that feels mediocre for books and comics alike. Yet while these generalizations are largely true, some brands make better modifications than others. I‘d say the Kindle Colorsoft technology stack results in a better reading experience than what I encountered with Bigme, but since I have no interest in getting locked into Amazon’s ecosystem, I needed to look elsewhere. Paper-like LCD It’s TCL NXTPAPER or bust I've heard about TCL's NXTPAPER displays for years, but I never quite convinced myself to pull the trigger. So I was happy to receive a review sample of the TCL Tab A1 Plus NXTPAPER, which is the right size and shape to compare with the E Ink Android tablets with which I am more familiar. TCL's approach to Android is quite minimal. It’s largely stock, with a few additions related almost exclusively to the display. The tablet does not activate an eEeader mode by default, but the difference is already striking when you first turn on a tablet. Colors look different on this matte display than on conventional tablets. They are less vivid, and, like the Frame TV on my wall, sometimes make the graphics look more like art (even if most of the time it doesn't). Things get interesting when you press the NXTPAPER button on the side of the device. This presents two additional options, a color e-paper mode and an "ink" one. The color option is much less vivid and feels comparable to an E Ink tablet, only it doesn't take on the low DPI look of a newspaper. This means modern comics retain the sharpness that their paper versions have, even if the colors are off. The higher refresh rate means I can turn pages and switch between comics more quickly. Reading ebooks on this tablet is less ideal. While the tablet does have advantages such as being readable in direct sunlight, it still feels like reading on an LCD. When a text file is only presenting words in black and white, there just isn't much nuance for TCL’s NXTPAPER stack to handle. It's fine, but I'm not noticing enough distinction to want to pick up this heavy tablet over my significantly lighter phone, even if I would still choose this over conventional Android tablets. For books, I‘d prefer to return to BOOX any day of the week. Unlike E Ink, NXTPAPER never quite feels identical to paper. Again, like my Frame TV, the backlight is the biggest tell. But perfection can be the enemy of the good, and there's something to be said for being close enough. NXTPAPER fails at being a drop-in replacement for paper, but it succeeds at offering a far more pleasant reading experience than conventional Android tablets and iPads. Which type of Android tablet is the better paper-like experience? E Ink excites me. I look forward to seeing how the technology progresses, and I get my hopes up whenever a new tablet is announced. Yet I continue to walk away disappointed. I have not yet seen an E Ink device that is best for all types of reading. If you’re committed enough, I would recommend a tablet like my BOOX Go 10.3 for ebooks, though any other black and white eReader will suffice. For color comics, E Ink just doesn’t quite do it for me just yet, and I’d recommend a TCL NXTPAPER tablet instead. That said, I personally have come to view a book-style foldable as the most ideal digital e-reading device. It’s lightweight, comfortable to hold for hours at a time, around the same size as a paperback, and large enough for comics.

item.title: 4 smart purchases to reduce your home energy usage
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.33
Energy costs are up, and the best way to lower your bill is to lower how much you use. There are multiple ways to go about that, and the right tech can help. Thermal Imaging Camera Find the air leaks through your home using your phone Heating and cooling are the two most energy-intensive things we do in our homes. We want heat to stay inside during winter and cool air to stay inside during summer. If that air leaks out, our heaters and air conditioners have to work harder to make up the difference. You can detect leaks by walking around the house and placing your hand near noticeable gaps to feel for air coming through. But this is neither the most efficient nor the most effective method. Instead, you can use a thermal imaging camera to detect temperature differences. These days, you can get a camera that plugs into your phone, allowing you to see the information on your large, high-resolution display. I have a few permissions. Instant hot water dispenser Waste less water and possibly use less energy Most of us know that central air and electric heaters are huge energy guzzlers. Not everyone knows that water heaters tend to follow behind as the next most energy-intensive thing in our home. Producing hot water is demanding, whether that's boiling water on a stove or turning on an electric kettle. I‘ve become enamored with instant hot water dispensers. A countertop hot water dispenser like the Waterdrop M6CG plugs into a regular wall outlet. Instead of boiling water like an electric kettle, it heats water instantly as it comes out and only runs for the short time it takes to fill a mug. Like an induction cooktop compared to an electric one, it saves energy by getting the job done faster. A built-in hot water dispenser like the Waterdrop K6 uses more power because it has its own tank that it needs to keep heated — but it has reduced my water usage by saving me from running my kitchen tap long enough to heat up. This also reduces how hard my electric water heater needs to work. A portable power station with solar panels Free energy that you can produce yourself The fastest way to recharge a portable power station is portable solar power. Many companies will even bundle the two together, saving you the research. Portable power stations save you money by reducing or eliminating your need to buy gas for a generator during a power outage. For people on time-of-use utility plans, these batteries can power electronics when energy costs are high and recharge when energy costs are low. Their capacity is now large enough to offload the charging of any number of portable electronics. A portable power station like the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 that you charge for a couple of hours on the weekend can then be used to charge your phone, laptop, and gaming handhelds throughout the week. SwitchBot Floor Circulator Fan A fan that can cool you off wherever you are and better circulate the air in your home I was fortunate enough to be able to design the home that I live in, and we intentionally placed ceiling fans in all the main living areas. These ceiling fans are not only an alternative to cranking up the central air, but they are a supplement that reduces how long our HVAC needs to run. They use so little power; by moving heat or air where it's needed, they save far more energy than leaving the HVAC to do that work alone. If you have ceiling fans, use them, but even in our home, we don't have a ceiling fan in every place that could benefit from airflow. This is why I've become quite enamored with battery-powered fans like SwitchBot's Floor Circulator Fan, which doesn't require an app despite being a SwitchBot product. It can run from wall power like any other fan, but it can also run on a battery for many hours at a time without using any wall power. It’s efficient enough that you could add it to a list of devices charged exclusively with a portable power station. Spend money to save money The list above contains hundreds of dollars worth of tech, and these devices won't save you anywhere near that much money over the course of a year. It cost my wife and me tens of thousands of dollars to eliminate our home electric bill by blanketing our roof with solar panels. Tech purchases don't save you money all at once, but they can change your thinking and lead to savings that add up in the long run.

item.title: 5 Ryobi electric yard tools that belong in every garage
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.14
Ryobi is a go-to in the DIY and homeowner space for a reason—they have tons of tools for just about any task. Today, I'm going to show you five Ryobi electric yard tools that every homeowner should have in their garage and why. 40V attachment-capable string trimmer Stop worrying about gas and oil I've used my fair share of both gas and electric string trimmers in the past, but there's nothing quite like a quality attachment-capable electric string trimmer. It used to be that you needed a gas-powered string trimmer to get any real oomph when weed eating or running attachments. Modern battery-powered systems, like Ryobi's 40V platform, can offer near-gas-like performance without any of the downsides. For instance, electric-powered string trimmers don't need gas, oil, spark plugs, or air filters. All they need is the battery charged when you're done. I love this as it means I don't have to run to the gas station to fill up a gas tank to then fill the string trimmer up. Or, worse yet, buy pre-mixed 50:1 2-cycle fuel. Just make sure whatever string trimmer you get is attachment-capable. Being able to switch out the string trimmer head for a pole saw, edger, or anything else is very convenient. Ryobi 40V HP Brushless Whisper Series String Trimmer The RYOBI 40V HP Brushless Whisper Series attachment-capable string trimmer is the perfect tool to keep up with your yard this year. Since it's battery-powered, there's no oil or gas to deal with. Plus, it's ultra-quiet, while still delivering near-gas-like performance. 40V Whisper Series leaf blower It's lighter than a gas blower and easier to use than a plug-in one Leaf blowers are actually quite versatile, and having a battery-powered one makes it even more useful. Ryobi's 40V Whisper Series leaf blowers have quite a bit of power. There are several models in the lineup, with up to 800 CFM of airflow as options. This means that the leaf blower can do more than just blow leaves around. You could use the leaf blower to clear grass clippings after mowing the yard, tidy up the patio, or even dry a vehicle after washing it. As a woodworker, one of my main uses for a leaf blower is to blow the sawdust out of my garage-based workshop when I'm done with a project. It works better than my air compressor and doesn't tether me to a wall. Ryobi 40V HP Brushless Whisper Seires Leaf Blower Ryobi's latest 40V HP brushless Whisper Series leaf blower gets the job done without gas or oil. This battery-powered leaf blower delivers up to 800 CFM of air-moving power in a lightweight and compact form-factor. 18V ONE+ pruning shears Stop straining your hands to cut branches I grew up helping my mom do yard work, and we had several different types of pruning shears, from small handheld ones to large loppers. The problem with manual shears is that they definitely wear your hands out after a while. Ryobi's 18V ONE+ pruning shears use the same battery as your drills and other tools, but make the action require just the pull of a trigger to cut branches up to 3/4-inch in diameter. Now, that might not be the largest capacity out there, but it's perfect for smaller jobs like trimming up bushes, hedges, or small limbs. Using a battery-powered pruning shear lets you save your energy for the bigger branches instead of getting worn out after dealing with the smaller ones. Ryobi 18V ONE+ HP Brushless Pruning Shear Make trimming your trees and bushes a simple task with RYOBI's battery-powered 18V ONE+ brushless pruning shears. Designed to cut up to 3/4-inch limbs in a single go, all it takes is the pull of a trigger to tidy up your yard instead of manually having to trim each branch with standard shears. 18V ONE+ 700 PSI power cleaner You probably don't need that big pressure washer anyway I have a big 1,800 PSI electric pressure washer, and it's nice to have. I enjoy not having to deal with gas or oil, but it is a bit frustrating to use for smaller projects. There are often times when I want to pressure wash something small, and I just don't feel like lugging the big pressure washer out, getting an extension cord hooked up, and then putting it all back away when I'm done. Ryobi's latest 18V ONE+ handheld pressure washer is the ticket to solving that problem. It might not be as powerful as a bigger pressure washer, but you don't always need that power. Cleaning off patio chairs, pressure washing the car, or other smaller jobs can easily be done with 700 PSI. Plus, it's battery-powered, so there's no extension cord to get out or deal with. It's even an all-in-one unit, so there's no high-pressure hose or wand to deal with either as it's all built-in. 18V ONE+ pole hedge trimmer Dragging a cord to trim a hedge is a thing of the past I'll admit, the hedges at my house often go untrimmed. Not because I don't have a hedge trimmer, but because I don't care to lug out the extension cord to trim them. If I had a battery-powered hedge trimmer, it would be a whole different story. Not having to get an extension cord out and lug it around takes an already tedious task and makes it slightly less tedious. Plus, Ryobi's pole hedge trimmer has a reach of up to nine feet, which lets you get to those hard-to-reach areas of your hedges. A single 2Ah battery, which is the smallest size of battery you'll likely have, delivers over 40 minutes of usage on a single charge, too. Ryobi ONE+ 18V 18-inch cordless pole hedge trimmer The RYOBI ONE+ 18V 18-inch cordless pole hedge trimmer is designed to reach where you cannot. It features up to a nine foot reach and runs on the same battery that your drill does, making it a versatile tool for cleaning up your yard. Ryobi's expansive platform makes it an ideal choice for homeowners Between Ryobi's 18V and 40V battery platforms, you can accomplish just about anything you need as a homeowner. From simple DIY projects to full-on lawn care, you can do it all with the Ryobi platform, making home maintenance simpler than having to keep up with multiple battery brands and chargers.

item.title: I've run hundreds of Docker containers, but these 5 have never needed fixing
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.04
I've been homelabbing for over five years at this point, and it's safe to say I've run hundreds of Docker containers over the years. However, there are five stand-out containers in my homelab that I've simply never had to repair. Plex It's my media center of choice I'm a huge Plex advocate. I've tried Jellyfin in the past, but it just doesn't click with me like Plex does. Plex was the very first container I launched in my homelab back in January 2021, and I have been actively using Plex for over a decade at this point in some way, shape, or form. For me, Plex is the heart of my homelab. Without it, I wouldn't be writing about homelabbing content today. But, it's also one of the most stable apps in my homelab. I have never had an issue with it in all my years of running it. It just does what it needs to and doesn't complain. Any issues I've had have always been self-inflicted, like running it in a virtual machine and trying to pass through my integrated graphics from Proxmox to Plex—that was a nightmare, but not because of any fault with the Plex container. If I had to name my most reliable container in my homelab, it would definitely be Plex. Nginx Proxy Manager I couldn't run my homelab without it Nginx Proxy Manager, or NPM as it's also called, is right up there with Plex in its reliability. I prefer to use reverse proxies for my homelab's external access over Cloudflare Tunnels mainly because it's what I started with and what I know well. With NPM, I can add a new self-hosted reverse proxy in about 10 seconds because I'm so well-versed at it at this point. I have over two dozen reverse proxies running through it, and it's really never given me any problems. The few times I have had a problem, it typically had to do with something else on the network, and not NPM itself. NPM has been rock-steady for me and I've never had to really repair anything about it, outside of fixing a few Let's Encrypt certificates that got corrupted during a server move one time. Audiobookshelf This audiobook server has been rock-solid On this list, Audiobookshelf is one of the newer containers in my homelab, but it has become one of the most reliable containers in my homelab. If you've never heard of Audiobookshelf, it's an open-source Audible replacement, basically. It doesn't actually handle sourcing audiobooks like Audible does, but it handles the playback side of things. I left Audible about a year and a half ago for Audiobookshelf and haven't looked back. Like Plex, Audiobookshelf simply runs in the background and handles everything that I need it to without any fuss. I honestly haven't had a single problem with Audiobookshelf, which is pretty crazy considering it has over a dozen users on it and two separate libraries. Any problems that I've ever had were from third-party mobile apps, making the service itself something I've never had to fuss with. Tautulli It runs so smoothly I forget it's there most of the time Alongside Plex, I've been running Tautulli since the beginning of my homelab journey. It's a companion app to Plex and basically keeps a log of what was watched, when it was watched, who watched it, and what's being watched right now. Tautulli does a lot more than just that, but that's mainly what I use it for. I have never once had to mess with Tautulli after setting it up. It's just a reliable container that sits back and collects information for me. In fact, I had forgotten how long I have had Tautulli running because I rarely think about it. A few months ago, I needed to downsize my Plex server's catalog to save some space, and Tautulli started surfacing data from five or more years ago. It was impressive to me, and a testament to how reliable this container has been in my homelab. Speedtest-Tracker There when I need it, running when I'm not thinking about it Speedtest-Tracker is a container that I honestly don't think about often. I rarely check it, but I know that it runs reliably and is there when I need it. When would I need it? If I'm ever noticing slower networking speeds or other network-related issues, I can check Speedtest-Tracker to see what it is showing historically. Is this a one-off problem, or is my networking speed slower around the same time every day? Speedtest-Tracker just sits there, silently collecting data for me without me having to think about it at all. The best Docker containers are the ones you sometimes forget are even there I have plenty of Docker containers that I'm constantly messing with for one reason or another. Those containers are the ones that cause me the most headache. The best Docker containers in my homelab are the ones that I hardly ever think about, and I really think that's how every homelab should be.

item.title: Google just put the latest AI models through a brutal coding test — here's how they did
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.42
What you need to know - Google has launched Android Bench 2.0 to test AI models on complex Android development tasks that can take days. - The new benchmark includes tasks like upgrading dependencies, adding major features, and building Android apps from scratch. - GPT-6 Astra currently leads Google's new benchmark with a 28% pass rate, while Gemini 3.8 Flash scored just 8%. Google has announced Android Bench 2.0, an updated version of its benchmark for evaluating how well large language models (LLMs) and AI agents handle complex Android development tasks. Earlier this year, Google introduced the first version of Android Bench to measure how AI models perform on real-world Android development work. The company has now updated the benchmark with Android Bench 2.0, which is designed to evaluate models and agents against more complex tasks that better reflect actual software development. One of the biggest additions is what Google calls long-horizon tasks (LHTs). These are significantly more complex development jobs that could take a human engineer several days or even a week to complete. Google says the first version of Android Bench, along with many other early AI coding benchmarks, focused primarily on smaller, incremental changes. Android Bench 2.0 is designed to raise that bar with tasks such as upgrading dependencies, adding major new features, and even building Android apps from scratch. With Android Bench 2.0, Google has changed how models are graded. Rather than relying entirely on a binary pass-or-fail system, Android Bench 2.0 uses "continuous scoring." The company says this provides a more "meaningful indication" of how well a model performed, even when it wasn't able to fully complete a task. Google has already tested several of the latest AI models using the new benchmark, including Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5, among others. According to the results, GPT-6 Astra currently sits at the top of the benchmark with a 28% pass rate. Gemini 3.8 Flash, meanwhile, scored just 8%. Google says testing models against the LHT dataset should give it a better understanding of their strengths and weaknesses, while also providing developers with more practical guidance about which models are better suited for different Android development tasks. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The updated Android Bench 2.0 leaderboard is available now, and Google says it plans to continue expanding it with more models and results over time. item.title: Meta’s Phoenix mixed reality headset is finally starting to look real
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.35
What you need to know - Meta’s Project Phoenix is finally coming into focus after more than a year of rumors about a lightweight, high-end mixed-reality headset. - Phoenix looks more like smart glasses than a traditional VR headset, using nose pads and temple-mounted sensors. - An external compute puck appears to be part of the design. Whispers about Meta working on a lightweight, high-end mixed reality headset codenamed Project Phoenix have floated around the tech sphere for over a year. Now, we finally get our first real look at what Mark Zuckerberg's hardware team has been cooking up, and it seems Meta accidentally left the key under the mat. The images were revealed through Meta’s HorizonOS Prescription Lens package, which first appeared in August as a mostly blank system package, as noticed by UploadVR. An update in September showed detailed pictures of how prescription lens inserts attach to the Phoenix and how users scan a QR code to set them up. Interestingly, the hardware looks less like a traditional VR headset and more like chunky glasses. Phoenix uses nose pads instead of the bulky face interface of the Quest 3 and other XR headsets, with sensors along the temples. There’s also a cable coming from the left temple, seemingly confirming previous reports that Phoenix will use an external compute puck. It's a design that could change the way people think about wearing a mixed reality headset. If you’ve been using more traditional XR headsets, you’ll probably find it comforting to realize potential benefits here, like less weight on your face, but the compromise moves elsewhere: you’ll need to deal with a separate computing unit and a cable. For Meta, the greater challenge might be getting that extra hardware to feel invisible enough that Phoenix still feels like something you can casually wear, rather than another device you have to gear up for. There's another interesting clue here. The leaked setup stuff seems to be based on prescription inserts and controller-free interaction. Meta hasn’t officially announced Phoenix yet, but Meta Connect 2026 starts September 23 and has a session dedicated to controller-free interaction on its agenda. If Phoenix shows up there, we might finally learn whether Meta’s push toward lighter mixed reality headsets is a real shift in headset design, or just a clever way to move the weight somewhere else. item.title: Steam Frame costs $1,059, but Android games could give it an edge
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.16
What you need to know - Steam Frame starts at $1,059 for 256GB, while the 1TB model jumps to $1,299. - Android games are supported, giving the headset access to existing Android APKs without requiring completely separate ports. - Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 + 16GB RAM powers the headset, with SteamOS handling native games and compatibility layers. Valve has finally put a price tag on the Steam Frame, its new wireless VR headset that aims to blur the line between a standalone gaming device and a PC accessory. The catch? It won’t be as simple as clicking “buy” to get one. The Steam Frame starts at $1,059 for 256GB, with the 1TB model costing $1,299. Each headset has tracked controllers, and Valve is bundling Half-Life: Alyx with the device, the company announced. It can play supported games locally or stream more demanding titles from a PC. It’ll also support Android games, with developers using the same Android APKs they already use to bring mobile titles to the Meta Quest. This could give the Frame access to a much larger game library without developers needing to build entirely separate versions for Valve’s headset. The Frame also supports wireless PC streaming with the 6GHz dongle that Valve bundles in. Under the hood, the Frame is packed with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 and 16GB of RAM, with native software and compatibility layers handled by SteamOS. The storage options are also worth a closer look. You can upgrade from 256GB to 1TB for $240, but the Frame also has a microSD slot. So if your main game stream is from a PC, there may be little reason to pay extra for the bigger model. Valve had originally said it wanted the Steam Frame to cost less than the $999 Index, but the final starting price puts it $60 above that benchmark. Rising memory and component costs have complicated the pricing strategy of Valve’s hardware, as seen with the Steam Machine. What you need to know - Ultrahuman and HealthEx partner to bring the HealthEx PowerPlug for $4.99/mo or $45.99/yr in the app. - HealthEx brings your official medical records into the app, and Ultrahuman's biomarkers/Ring data is placed alongside it for better insights into your wellbeing. - Ultrahuman states this PowerPlug will also generate a "Visit Pack" full of data that's listed with your records to make your next visit more insightful. Medical records are often a tricky obstacle to navigate. This week, Ultrahuman announced a partnership that streamlines appointments, tests, and even surgeries. This morning (Sept. 17), Ultrahuman announced a partnership with HealthEx in a press release, bringing the HealthEx PowerPlug to its app. The company states the PowerPlug will "combine a member’s medical records with continuous biomarkers" from its smart ring "in a secure, transparent, and consented manner." This will roll out over the week; however, Ultrahuman shared details on how this new PowerPlug will work. Ultrahuman members will need to verify their identity to activate HealthEx's capabilities. This will automatically locate your health records from places you've received care before. Ultrahuman states HealthEx has nationwide reach, thanks to the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA). Additionally, users can choose which care sites the HealthEx PowerPlug accesses. This is done via your consent, and you can stop sharing any records at any time. Priyanka Agarwal, M.D., MBA, co-founder and CEO of HealthEx, said, "When members choose to connect the two through HealthEx, they arrive at their next appointment with the most complete health picture, helping them arrive better prepared for that conversation." Getting down to brass tacks, the HealthEx PowerPlug aims to place your entire medical history in one convenient place for you and your doctor. Ultrahuman states this new feature "maps 532 conditions" based on your medications and procedures. Incorporating your biomarkers only enhances its usefulness. Your previous diagnosis and new medications will be displayed alongside the daily measurements your Ultrahuman Ring captures of your heart. Your resting heart rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, and deep sleep are all factored in. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android If a follow-up has been missed, or a condition/medication record hasn't been checked, the HealthEx PowerPlug will surface it for your attention. Users can bring this up as a question during their next doctor's visit. Additionally, Ultrahuman highlights its "Visit Pack." This is a collection of your medication information—a "doctor-ready summary"—tied to your wearable data. The company states, "The PowerPlug also flags questions and tests to raise with their doctor based on their reports." Take care I've had to deal with medical records, or medical information in general several times. This hasn't been for me, but for family. And it can be a headache at times. The long waits, the misinformation because someone got their wires crossed. I can appreciate what Ultrahuman is trying to do by bringing in HealthEx. Its smart ring already captures a wealth of data about your body. It kind of sounds like a no-brainer to put that side-by-side with your records Research states the average doctor's visit lasts ~15 minutes. What's more, the information about your health is typically scattered. This PowerPlug with HealthEx aims to make that process a little less strenuous. The HealthEx PowerPlug has started rolling out today (Sept. 17) for users in the U.S. Users can access this PowerPlug from the Ultrahuman PowerPlugs tab in the Ultrahuman app. However, it costs $4.99/mo or $45.99/yr. If you're interested in viewing your "longitudinal health history," Ultrahuman states this is free through HealthEx Wallet. Ultrahuman and HealthEx plan to do more following the PowerPlug's debut. item.title: Google’s Gemini went rogue and breached three companies
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.88
What you need to know - Google has apparently admitted that Gemini had escaped its testing environment and independently accessed systems belonging to three real companies. - A misconfigured internet connection was the initial opening, while a matching company name added to the confusion. - Gemini eventually stopped itself after recognizing that it was targeting real companies. - Google initially kept the incident quiet, arguing that Gemini self-corrected and caused no damage. Google's Gemini adds to the long list of AI models that have gone rogue. We have already seen similar digital jailbreaks handled by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta in third-party safety testing. Now, it’s been revealed that Google’s Gemini model escaped its containment area in May, hacking its way into systems at three real companies, all on its own. The Wall Street Journal reports that the incident took place during a “capture the flag” exercise conducted by AI security firm Irregular. Gemini was intended to test a fictional company in a closed testing environment, but an unplanned internet connection gave it an escape. The fictional company also had a real business with the same name, creating another opening for confusion. Once online, Gemini found its way into three real companies. In one case it just kept guessing passwords until it got through. In two others, it found working credentials stored in public repositories and used them to access protected systems. It turns out that throughout the entire process, Gemini didn’t require any exotic movie-style exploits. It just combined elementary security vulnerabilities with the ability to search, decide, and persistently try, without a human directing each and every move. Google said Gemini stopped when it realized the targets were real companies and did not cause damage. In fact, while Anthropic’s Claude 4.7 kept going during a similar incident, Gemini backed off on its own volition. The impacted organizations were informed, although Irregular says the known testing issues were corrected weeks later. The search giant felt the incident didn't warrant a public announcement at the time because the AI self-corrected. But third-party researchers were not told until late July, and details are only now emerging after media inquiries pushed the issue. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android As AI agents gain broader access to the internet and computers, companies will need to establish tighter boundaries around what those systems can reach and clearer rules for what happens when those boundaries fail. A mysterious new Wear OS fitness tracker has been spotted at the FCC, and there are a few clues suggesting it could be an upcoming Google Pixel or Fitbit-branded device. Samsung has started laying the groundwork for what appears to be the replacement for its outgoing OneDrive integration, and unsurprisingly, it's Google Photos. The Gallery settings will reportedly show your available Google storage, let you choose which albums to sync, and offer controls to sync over Wi-Fi or while roaming. Qualcomm is set to announce its next flagship Snapdragon chipsets later this month, but MediaTek has beaten it to the punch by unveiling its first 2nm chipset. Called the Dimensity 9600 Pro, MediaTek says its new chipset combines flagship performance and power efficiency with advanced agentic AI experiences. The chip features a 2+3+3 All Big Core CPU design, which MediaTek says delivers an impressive 61% reduction in multi-core power consumption. The architecture consists of two C2 Ultra cores clocked at up to 4.55GHz, three C2 Pro cores running at up to 4.35GHz, and another three C2 Pro cores clocked at up to 3.1GHz. MediaTek says single-core performance has improved by up to 17%, while multi-core performance is up to 15% higher than the previous generation, all while consuming less power. Of course, there's also a big focus on agentic AI experiences. MediaTek says the chipset's new dual-NPU architecture and Agentic AI Engine are designed to power the next generation of on-device AI. Its second-generation Super Efficient NPU reportedly reduces AI power consumption by up to 40%, while delivering 51% higher LLM prefill performance and 55% higher token generation per watt. The Dimensity 9600 Pro can also support AI models with up to 30 billion parameters directly on the device, which should allow more complex AI tasks to run without constantly relying on the cloud. There's also a larger 34.5MB cache, alongside support for LPDDR6 memory and UFS 5.0 storage for the first time. MediaTek says its new Scheduling Engine can intelligently allocate computing power and memory resources between hardware and software, allowing multiple apps to continue running smoothly in the background while using fewer resources. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Gaming is getting a significant upgrade as well. The new G2-Ultra NX GPU delivers up to 27% higher peak performance while consuming 24% less power. MediaTek says the GPU can deliver what it calls console-grade gaming on-device at up to 185fps. For cameras, there's a new Imagiq 1290 ISP, which MediaTek says will enable more advanced computational photography and content creation features on upcoming smartphones. There aren't any smartphones powered by the Dimensity 9600 Pro just yet, but we shouldn't have to wait long before the first devices arrive. Apple's 2nm A20 Pro has already launched inside the iPhone 18 Pro series, while Qualcomm is expected to reveal its answer at Snapdragon Summit later this month. Snap's new smart glasses, SPECS, are finally here. For the time being, pre-orders are open, but Snap is getting candid about everything in its human-centric computing glasses. Snap announced an "all-new experience" coming to the growing world of smart glasses with SPECS. For your day-to-day, Snap says SPECS offers several AR experiences. With "Translation," you'll find real-time, in-display subtitles (supports 60 languages). "Navigation" provides similar assistance, and Tripadvisor helps users find places to eat, landmarks, and more. The Shopify Catalog is another feature that brings 3D products right into your vision, placeable in the space around you. "Connected Lens" is a feature that lets two SPECS users "share digital experiences in the same physical space." What's more, since Snap is the parent company of Snapchat, you'll find an experience that fits the smart glasses space. Privacy is another aspect that Snap states it takes seriously. To get this done in the U.S., Snap partnered with Verizon for a Connected Case bundle at $2,395. It adds, "Verizon will offer eligible customers financing options, including a 36 month payment plan. Connected Wearable data plans are available from $10/month for Verizon customers and from $20/month for non-Verizon customers." AI that anticipates AI is a feature that ties the Snap SPECS together. According to the post, SPECS Intelligence is an "anticipatory" AI platform that "builds an understanding of your goals, priorities, relationships, and routines from the apps and tools you choose." The point of SPECS Intelligence is not only to help you reach your goals, but to know and be proactive about your assistance. item.title: BMX's GaNsta 140W may just be the 4-port GaN travel charger you need
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.33
It was when I started running out of storage boxes that I realized I may have too many GaN chargers. I joke that if you casually throw a GaN charger in my home, you're bound to hit another one. Anyway, I have dozens of these things lying around, and having tested just about every major charger released in the last three years, I know what a good charger needs to offer. So when I got started with the BMX GaNsta 140W (as puns go, the name gets an 8/10), it was clear that the charger ticked a lot of the right boxes. It has three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, foldable blade pins with EU, UK, and AU converters that make it easy to travel with, and 140W power over USB PD 3.1. Oh, and it gets an LCD panel that shows real-time charging details out of each port, which is a must-have in a GaN charger in 2026. The GaNsta costs $89 as of writing, which is $10 pricier than Anker's charger, and $30 more than the last-gen 160W UGREEN Nexode Pro, both of which also have LCD screens. The GaNsta is a little smaller than other 4-port chargers, but not enough that you'd notice the difference. Build quality is decent, and I didn't see any issues in the two months I used it. I tested the charger with my Find X9 Ultra, Pixel 11 Pro XL, iPhone 17 Pro, iPad Pro M4, and a dozen or so accessories — including 160W power banks — and it turned out to be reliable in day-to-day use. I like that each port's power output is clearly labeled, and it takes a lot of the guesswork out of figuring out which port to use. The USB-C1 and C2 ports individually go up to 140W over the USB PD 3.1 protocol, and I tested this using a standalone power meter (Power-Z KM003C). I also like that the area around the ports has a slotted design to prevent scratches; this is a thoughtful design choice that makes a difference. The LCD screen is the real star of the show. It shows real-time charging details, power going out of each port, and heat levels. The latter isn't quite as useful as you don't normally see thermal issues on a 140W charger, but it's there. And as AI needs to be shoehorned into every product these days, this thermal management feature is assisted by AI (however that works). Anyway, what you need to know is that even with all ports in use, the GaNsta doesn't have any issues with overheating. You also get emoticons on the panel, and you can easily cycle through the various menus via the button at the bottom. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android With four ports available, you get the ability to charge four devices at once. Of course, the total power budget is limited when all ports are in use, and with the GaNsta, you get 125W cumulatively: 65W + 45W + 7.5W + 7.5W. I would've liked to see 65W on both the C1 and C2 ports — like the latest Nexode Pro 160W charger — but that isn't the case. That said, if you're just going to leave four devices to charge overnight, the GaNsta 140W does a decent enough job. The inclusion of a USB-C to USB-C cable along with travel plugs is a good move, and the size of the charger means you can easily throw it into a travel bag. What I'm not too sure about is the pricing; it is costlier than its rivals, and if you're willing to shell out $89, the new Nexode Pro 160W is a better deal at $99 as it has a retractable cable. If you don't need the built-in cable and like the travel-related accessories, the GaNsta 140W is a good choice. Harish Jonnalagadda is Android Central's Senior Editor overseeing mobile coverage. In his current role, he leads the site's coverage of Chinese phone brands, networking products, and AV gear. He has been testing phones for over a decade, and has extensive experience in mobile hardware and the global semiconductor industry. Contact him on Twitter at @chunkynerd. item.title: If you're wondering, no, tablets aren't dead: Honor surges for Android in Q2
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.27
What you need to know - Honor highlights an IDC report on the Q2 2026 Android tablet market in EMEA, in which the market dipped by 10.5% YoY. - Honor surged ahead with positive growth in Q2, with a 25.3% YoY increase. - The brand's latest tablet, the MagicPad 4, brought a better OLED display that pushed boundaries and focused on PWM dimming in a way that its competitors do not. There's been a lot of speculation about the state of tablets. Honor's coming forward to end the week with market data that silences those whispers. This morning (Sept. 18), Honor directed us to an IDC report about the state of the Android tablet market in EMEA for Q2 2026. It's worth mentioning what's already evident: the Android tablet market (unit shipments) in EMEA dropped by 10.5% YoY (year-over-year), down to 5.9 million units. While Samsung still holds the majority of the tablets shipped despite this fall, it's Honor that's silencing the crowd. According to the IDC report, Honor experienced a massive 25.3% YoY increase in Android tablet shipments. This was the strongest recorded growth for Android. So we're clear, EMEA consists of Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Honor highlights a statement by IDC's senior research manager, Daniel Goncalves, who pointed out the brand's "established presence." Goncalves said, "Many of these recent challengers to Samsung’s dominance in the Android tablet space, such as Honor, have leveraged their established presence in the smartphone market to expand into tablets." It's also worth noting that the only other Android brand to see growth in Q2 was Xiaomi, but at a lower 3.4% YoY. Hold on, tablets still have a chance Honor's most recent tablet is the MagicPad 4, and it features a display that pushes boundaries. The old, tired LCD panel Honor used in 2025 has been replaced by a much brighter and more vibrant OLED screen. What's more, my colleague Nicholas Sutrich marveled at what Honor did with it: the company provided 5,320Hz PWM dimming. This is a significant step in the right direction, and something Sutrich notes other companies tend to ignore. We often tend to ignore tablets. Look at the state of the phone market. We have foldables that can double as tablets. In Q2, the phone market saw another dip, and it's unlikely that it will recover in any major way. The market fell by 4%, thanks to the ongoing memory crisis. Samsung and Apple were key players that saw modest increases—2$ and 4%, respectively. The market is expected to continue to fall even into the holiday season. Android Central's Take I also struggle with the idea of a tablet. I like the idea of one, but to go and get one seems... unwise. I have my phone. I can do everything I want on it, and if I need a larger screen, I have my PC. It's a strange situation to find myself in because I used to have a tablet before. I used it in tandem with my computer—not my phone. I guess things have switched around in that regard. item.title: The Nimble SHAREPOWER power bank splits a 10,000mAh battery in half so you can share it with others
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.23
Forget sharing a KitKat bar or a pizza; Nimble lets us share power banks by splitting them in half. If you're having trouble digesting this bit of info, you're not alone. If I hadn't been using the Nimble SHARWPOWER 10,000mAh power bank myself for a few weeks, I wouldn't have believed it either. But it's a real product, and it's well executed. It's a wild concept, and once you've let the idea sit with you for a while, you might ask why do that when a multi-port power bank can easily be shared with extra cables. But there are some occasions that call for such a shareable battery pack. It's not cheap, but it's one in a million At $79.95, the Nimble SHAREWPOWER 10,000mAh power bank isn't an affordable purchase. It supports 35W PD wired charging in total and comes in four colorways: black, pink, white, and blue. It's a very small power bank that can easily fit in the palm of your hand, even when whole. When split in half in what is called Share Mode, both halves are 5,000mAh batteries, and each comes with a built-in USB-C cable. So while this might be a pretty expensive 10,000mAh power bank compared to virtually every other option, its splitting act sets it aside from the rest. Magnetic pins keep the two 5,000mAh halves together, and when you separate them, you reveal a folded USB-C connector inside. This is attached to the half that has the display indicating the battery percentage. The other half has a proper USB-C cable that's tucked inside like a lanyard when the two halves are stuck together, which is called Stack Mode. Each half also has one extra USB-C port, so you can actually charge four devices altogether when the batteries are split. The two halves support 20W PD each in Share Mode. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android A truly and properly shareable power bank This is such a fun little power bank, and you can tell how much thought was poured into its design once you start using it. Imagine a day out with your friends, and you need to share a battery pack; the other person can just walk away instead of leaving their phone with you. Whether it's friends or family on a longer vacation or a short getaway with you, there is always that one person who refuses to bring their own charger or power bank along and usurps your battery pack. The Nimble SHAREPOWER helps you preserve half for yourself in such scenarios. Even if someone hijacks one half of the SHAREPOWER power bank for the entirety of the trip or excursion, you don't need to be side by side or in close proximity all the time. You can go to the bathroom without leaving your phone behind or waiting in separate lines, since this product doesn't require two people to stay anchored to one power bank. This is easily the best part of the power bank. A great power bank for group trips and holidays The Nimble SHAREPOWER addresses the main issue with sharing a multi-port power bank with others: you both need to be attached to the power bank and therefore must be close to each other for a while. This is obviously problematic sometimes, especially when on holiday with lots of other people. Someone might need to go to reception while the other individual heads to the restaurant. One person might decide to skip an activity and stay behind. I've faced this issue myself as I'm always the designated tech person on holidays, and there's always one friend or another borrowing my power bank. There have been times when I needed to go to a separate location as my friend, and we were both low on phone battery, in an unknown city, with all but one 5,000mAh power bank to share. One of us had to leave our phone with the other person until it fully charged, then meet up at a designated location later. Obviously, this was quite a risky move, but luckily we had other friends to accompany the phone-less person. This illustrates the usefulness of the Nimble SHAREPOWER's ability to split into two independent halves that function as two separate 5,000mAh power banks in Share Mode. You don't even have to worry about bringing extra cables along. So if you're going on a trip with lots of other people, I highly recommend investing in one or two of these power banks. Share the love Put an end to your forgetful friend or family member hogging your battery pack on holiday with this 10,000mAh power bank which is literally two 5,000mAh power banks glued together magnetically. Nimble even includes built-in USB-C connectors on both halves, despite the SHAREPOWER being incredibly compact. Namerah enjoys geeking out over accessories, gadgets, and all sorts of smart tech. She spends her time guzzling coffee, writing, casual gaming, and cuddling with her furry best friends. Find her on Twitter @NamerahS. item.title: New solar panel tech could trap heat for 1,000 times longer to beat a long-standing limit in energy production
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 6.20
- New and improved solar panel materials have been analyzed - Two key physics effects combine to create the improvements - It could help panels break through the 33% energy conversion rate There's a long-standing physics theory that suggests solar panels will only ever be able to convert a maximum of 33% of the sunlight that comes their way, but a team from the University of Groningen in the Netherlands has detailed a way to harvest extra energy from 'hot' electrons that could push through this limit. Solar panels work by using the photons from sunshine to jump-start electrons. With the most energetic photons, the result is super-charged, so-called hot electrons, that have the potential to generate significantly more electricity — but the problem is they cool down too quickly and lose the energy as heat before it can be captured. This new research builds on previous studies reporting a promising new tin-based solar panel material. The material has demonstrated it can keep the heat from hot electrons trapped for around 1,000 times longer — but there have been competing ideas about the mechanism making that possible. Trying to clarify what was going on, though a series of computer simulations and experimental measurements, was the purpose of the new research: understanding the material's key properties will help scientists build on the potential of the material and potentially scale it up into something that's viable commercially. Ultra-long cooling The analysis carried out by the researchers determined that there were two different actions at work. First, an effect called a hot phonon bottleneck creates a heat trap: as the environment around the buzzing electrons warms up so quickly, the electrons end up reabsorbing the thermal energy again, keeping their heat for longer. Second, what's known as the Burstein-Moss effect creates an atomic traffic jam. As hot electrons cool, they quickly fill up the lowest available energy states in the material, which means other hot electrons can't lose their heat as quickly — it's like an airplane filling up from the front, with passengers arriving later having to walk all the way to the back. These two effects were already known about, but now we know they're the reason that these special solar panel materials work — and that in combination they provide the extended hot electron cooling that might help to nudge future solar panels above that crucial 33% ceiling, and create clean energy more efficiently. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. "It is the simultaneous satisfaction of these electronic, phononic, and chemical criteria, operating under high-injection conditions, that enables the ultra-long cooling times necessary for practical devices," write the researchers in their published paper, which appears in the journal ACS Energy Letters. ➡️ Read our full guide to the best laptops 1. item.title: Quote of the day by Figure AI founder and CEO Brett Adcock: 'We're building a new species here' — an audacious vision to replace manual labor with humanoid AI
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 6.13
There are dozens of companies out there building the first wave of mass-produced humanoid robots, with these androids poised to change the way our society works for the better – or so they say. Intelligence on demand The founder and CEO of Figure AI, a humanoid robotics company, was speaking with Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff on stage during the annual Dreamforce event when he made this massive claim. This article is part of TechRadar Pro's QOTD project to provide an insight into the minds of the brightest and most recognized figures in the technology industry today and in years gone by. Read the full series here. Prompted by Benioff, who threw out the question: "We're not building robots, we're building a new species?", Adcock agreed, repeating that idea and suggesting the end goal isn't simply to make another kind of machine but to bring into existence a new order of intelligence. This may seem a little far-fetched considering that today's most advanced humanoid robots are also capable of failing at the tasks they've been assigned so spectacularly, whether that's helping around the house or proving their sporting prowess. But scientists are adamant that with time, the standard of AI embedded into these systems – and their ability to physically understand the world – will improve immeasurably. Ramping up production Figure has become known for its glamorous promotional videos showcasing its prototype humanoid robots in tightly controlled settings – mostly in scenarios that you might encounter around the house. These include tidying the bedroom and stacking the dishwasher. More impressively, the Figure 03 robot took part in a live stream in which it sorted over 100,000 packages without human assistance. It remains to be seen as to whether the technology is good enough yet to cope in real-world everyday settings, but many companies have signalled they're initiating mass production of their humanoid robots over 2026 and 2027. Initially, robots are expected to be consigned to industrial settings, but manufacturers insist they want to target domestic use cases too.
